domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk focuses on building a realtime voice AI agent with an STT-LM-TTS pipeline, RAG, and telephony integration for phone-based customer support. Fin Voice is an enterprise customer support product automating phone-based customer service interactions. Fin Voice was built in ~100 days and deployed to several enterprise customers on their main phone lines. The talk covers practical engineering and product decisions for practitioners familiar with AI systems concepts. Recorded conference presentation at AI Engineer World's Fair. All evidence anchors are direct quotes from the transcript with grade 'said_in_transcript'.

summary: Peter Bar presents Fin Voice, Intercom's AI voice agent for phone customer support, built in roughly 100 days and deployed to several enterprise customers on their main phone lines. Intercom, already known for its messenger and chat-based AI agent Fin (serving 5,000+ customers with 56% average resolution rate, some at 70-80%), extended Fin to voice. Bar argues voice remains critical: over 80% of support teams use phone support, one-third of customer service interactions occur by phone, and human-handled US calls cost $7-12—voice AI can be at least 5x cheaper while offering 24/7 availability, no wait times, no IVR menus, and multilingual support across 30-40+ languages. The team chose a flexible knowledge-based agent answering help article questions rather than narrow use cases, validated by chat data and call transcript analysis. Out-of-office-hours support was the initial wedge use case. The MVP prioritized three experiences: a playground (shipped within 4 weeks), deployment configuration, and observability tools. The tech stack uses a chained STT-to-LM-to-TTS loop with OpenAI's realtime API, RAG, and telephony integration. Conversation design for voice required rethinking chat assumptions around latency (~1s for simple queries, filler words for complex ones), answer chunking with user confirmation, and user mindset adaptation from IVR-like to natural speech. Support team workflow integration proved surprisingly critical—feedback focused more on workflow fit than model quality. Key features included escalation paths and context handoff via transcript summaries for human agents. Evaluation combined manual and automated test conversation sets on every major code change, internal tooling for reviewing logs and recordings, resolution rate as the northstar metric (user confirms resolution or disconnects after one answer without calling back within 24 hours), and experimental LLM-as-a-judge for transcript analysis. Cost ranges 3-20 cents per minute depending on query complexity and providers. Two pricing models dominate: usage-based (predictable but misaligned incentives) and outcome-based (charging only for resolved issues, better aligned but carrying provider risk). Bar expects market convergence toward outcome-based pricing. His key takeaway: achieving performance is not just a model problem but a product problem—requiring the right use case, conversation design, tooling, workflow integration, and trust-building with support teams.

sections.title: Introduction to Fin Voice
sections.summary: Peter Bar introduces Fin Voice, Intercom's AI voice agent for phone support that picks up calls, answers questions, and escalates to human agents. Built in approximately 100 days, positioned as the next frontier in AI customer service.

sections.title: Intercom Context and Fin Chat Success
sections.summary: Intercom is a customer service platform and AI agent company. Launched Fin chat agent two years ago after GPT-4, now serving 5,000+ customers with 56% average resolution rate (up to 70-80% for some). Fin includes continuous optimization tooling for analyzing, training, testing, and deploying.

sections.title: Why Voice?
sections.summary: Voice is the preferred channel for urgent or sensitive issues. Over 80% of support teams use phone support, one-third of interactions are phone-based. Human calls cost $7-12 in the US; voice AI can be 5x cheaper. Benefits include 24/7 availability, no wait times, no IVR menus, multilingual support (30-40+ languages), cost savings, and scalability.

sections.title: Seven Areas Overview
sections.summary: Bar outlines seven main areas that had the biggest impact on building Fin Voice: use case, MVP scope, tech stack, conversation design, support team integration, evaluation, and pricing.

sections.title: Use Case Selection
sections.summary: Chose a flexible knowledge-based agent over narrow use cases (scheduling, booking), validated by chat Fin data and call transcript analysis showing most queries solvable with help articles. Initial wedge: out-of-office-hours support replacing voicemail. Other use cases considered: authentication, info gathering, smart routing.

sections.title: MVP: What They Shipped First
sections.summary: Three core experiences: Fin Voice playground (lightweight test environment shipped within 4 weeks), deploy experience (configuration for agent behavior and workflows), and observability/monitoring (transcripts, recordings, summaries, call outcomes for customer service agents).

sections.title: Tech Stack
sections.summary: Core loop: STT to LM to TTS. Considered voice-to-voice models (faster, more natural, less control) but started with and retained realtime API. RAG critical for knowledge base answers. Telephony for phone line integration. Had head start from existing chat RAG and native phone support product.

sections.title: Conversation Design for Voice
sections.summary: Three key differences from chat: latency (1s target for simple queries, filler words for complex 3-4s queries), answer length (chunked delivery with user confirmation between steps for multi-step responses), and user mindset (customers start with IVR-like single-word interactions but adapt to full sentences mid-conversation).

sections.title: Support Team Workflow Integration
sections.summary: Workflow integration became the biggest blocker for enterprise deployment, not model quality or latency. Two key features: escalation paths for configuring how calls get escalated to human agents, and context handoff via transcript summaries generated after every AI call to give human agents full context of what happened.

sections.title: Evaluation
sections.summary: Four evaluation approaches: (1) manual and automated test conversation sets run on every major code change, (2) internal streamed web apps for reviewing logs, transcripts, and recordings to troubleshoot customer issues, (3) resolution rate as northstar metric—user confirms resolution or disconnects after one answer without calling back within 24 hours, (4) experimental LLM-as-a-judge analyzing call transcripts to identify issues and improvement opportunities.

sections.title: Pricing
sections.summary: Cost ranges 3-20 cents per minute depending on query complexity and providers chosen. Two dominant pricing models: usage-based (per minute or per call, predictable but misaligned incentives) and outcome-based (charge only for resolved issues, better aligned incentives but provider absorbs cost of long unresolved calls). Bar expects market convergence toward outcome-based pricing.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
sections.summary: Recap: built and shipped Fin Voice in ~100 days with several enterprise customers on main phone lines. Key takeaway: achieving performance in latency and resolution is not just a model problem but a product problem—requiring right use case selection, conversation design for phone realities, internal and external tooling, workflow integration, and trust-building with support teams who decide whether to release it. Goal is making it feel effortless despite behind-the-scenes complexity.
